newsitem.title: USA: Lithuanians held in U.S. on nuclear weapons charges. [CORRECTED 00:40 GMT 1/7]
newsitem.headline: Lithuanians held in U.S. on nuclear weapons charges. [CORRECTED 00:40 GMT 1/7]

text.p: Two Lithuanian men have been arrested in Miami on charges of plotting to sell nuclear and other weapons to U.S. undercover agents posing as Colombian drug dealers, customs officials said on Monday.
(Corrects nationality of men from Russian to Lithuanian.)
No weapons were actually delivered, Dennis Fagan, acting special agent in charge of the Miami Customs region, said.

The suspects, Alexander Progrebeshski and Alexander Darichev, pleaded not guilty before a federal magistrate on Monday on charges of conspiring to ship explosive materials and missiles without a license and conspiring to unlawfully transfer nuclear materials.

Both were ordered jailed without bond. The suspects were arrested on Friday afternoon at a hotel near the U.S. Customs office in Miami and mistakenly described earlier on Monday as Russians by a customs spokesman.

Customs agents arrested the pair before they could complete the shipment of Russian Strela and Igla missiles to Puerto Rico because investigators worried the shipment would go astray. The missiles are shoulder-fired, portable, surface-to-air missiles commonly known in the West as the SAM-14 (Strela) and SAM-16 (Igla).
"We could not guarantee the safety or integrity of the weapons," Fagan said.
Under the deal, the agents were to pay up front for the weapons and the suspects planned to leave the country before the arms arrived.
"We did not want the two to leave the United States," Fagan said.

The investigation began in March 1995 as a probe of stolen cars by the Odessa Joint Task Force, made up of numerous south Florida police and federal agencies investigating mobsters from the former Soviet Union dubbed "Redfellas."

According to an arrest affidavit, the suspects offered agents at meetings in Miami and London a shopping list of shoulder-fired and other surface-to-air missiles for sale. They produced brochures describing Russian Strela and Igla missiles.
Richard Gregorie, a senior litigation counsel with the U.S. Attorney's Office, said one discussion involved "40 missiles for $1 million."

"They also asked us at that time if we were interested in any nuclear weapons. This of course aroused our attention," Fagan said. Investigators refused to describe the nuclear weapons or their source except to say they were "tactical nuclear weapons."
The suspects said the weapons would be supplied by Armimex, a Bulgarian government-owned munitions supplier that had been licensed by the former USSR to produce Soviet weapons during the Cold War.
The agents recorded phone conversations with a man who claimed to be an Armimex agent, and with the owner of the cargo ship Al Fares, which was registered in Equatorial Guinea.

Ship owner Angelo Zeini offered to ship the weapons from Bourgas, Bulgaria, to Puerto Rico in a load of "cheap junk materials" that would pass inspection at the Straits of Gibraltar, the affadavit said.
He sought $330,000 to make the shipment and falsify documents identifying them as machinery and "general cargo" bound for Puerto Rico.
